title: Maximum Hamming Distances
statement:
The Hamming distance of two integers is the number of bit positions in which their binary forms differ.

You get an array `nums` and an integer `m`, and every value satisfies `0 <= nums[i] < 2^m`, so each one is an `m`-bit number. Return an array `answer` of the same length where `answer[i]` is the largest Hamming distance between `nums[i]` and any element `nums[j]` with `j != i`. Values may repeat, and the array always has at least two elements.
notes:
## Intuition

Comparing every pair costs O(n²), and `n` can reach 2^17. Flip the question around: the distance from `x` to `y` is `m` minus the distance from `~x` (all `m` bits flipped) to `y`. So the farthest element from `x` is the one nearest to its complement, and "nearest element of `nums`" for every `m`-bit value is exactly what a multi-source BFS over the hypercube computes, where neighbours differ in one bit.

## Approach

1. Make `dist` of size `2^m`, filled with `-1` (unvisited).
2. Put every distinct value of `nums` in the `queue` with distance `0`.
3. Pop `node`; for each `bit`, the neighbour `next = node ^ (1 << bit)` gets `dist[node] + 1` the first time it is seen.
4. When the BFS ends, `dist[v]` is the smallest Hamming distance from `v` to any element.
5. For each `num`, the answer is `m - dist[num ^ mask]`, where `num ^ mask` is its complement.

An element at distance 0 from itself never lowers the result: it is the farthest possible point from the complement, so another element always does at least as well.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [9, 12, 9, 11]`, `m = 4`, `mask = 15`. The sources are 9 (1001), 12 (1100) and 11 (1011). The complement of 9 is 6 (0110); its nearest source is 12 (1100 vs 0110 differ in 2 bits), so `dist[6] = 2` and the answer is `4 - 2 = 2`. The complement of 12 is 3 (0011), one bit from 11 (1011), so the answer is `4 - 1 = 3`. The complement of 11 is 4 (0100), one bit from 12, giving 3. Result: `[2, 3, 2, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^m · m): each of the `2^m` values is queued once and tries `m` bit flips.
- Space: O(2^m) for `dist` and the queue.

## Pitfalls

- Flip only the low `m` bits (`num ^ mask`); JavaScript's `~num` would give a negative number.
- Seed the BFS with every element at once; running one BFS per element is far too slow.
- Duplicates are fine: the second copy is already marked and is skipped.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | number of `m`-bit values, `2^m` |
| `mask` | `m` one-bits, used to take the complement |
| `dist` | smallest Hamming distance from each value to an element of `nums` |
| `num` | an element of `nums` |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and its read position |
| `node`, `next` | the value being expanded and a neighbour one bit away |
| `bit` | the bit position flipped to reach `next` |

narration.2: There are 2^m possible m-bit values, the vertices of the hypercube.
narration.3: A mask of m one-bits lets us flip every bit of a value.
narration.4: Every value starts unvisited, marked with -1.
narration.6: Every element of nums is a BFS source.
narration.7: Skip a value already queued, so duplicates are handled once.
narration.8: An element is at distance 0 from itself.
narration.12: Process the queue in order, so distances grow level by level.
narration.14: Try flipping each of the m bits.
narration.15: The neighbour differs from node in exactly one bit.
narration.16: Only the first visit counts, because BFS reaches each value by a shortest path.
narration.17: The neighbour is one bit farther from the nearest element than node.
narration.22: The farthest element from num is the nearest one to its complement, so subtract that distance from m.
